opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few things going on, and some of it is a bit accidental.

One part is the training process. When you do RLHF, you're collecting preferences from raters who are comparing two responses side by side. In that setting, a longer, more thorough answer often looks better. It seems like it covered more ground, it has more caveats, it anticipated more follow-up questions. So the rater picks it, even if a real user in the middle of their actual work would have preferred something shorter. You end up optimizing for how a response looks when someone's carefully evaluating it, which isn't quite the same as what's most useful in practice.

Another part is that the model doesn't know much about who it's talking to or what they need. If you don't know whether the person is an expert or a beginner, or whether they want the one-line answer or the full explanation, the safe move is to hedge and cover everything. Verbosity is partly a symptom of uncertainty about the user. As models get better at picking up context, or have memory of who you are, I'd expect that to improve.

There's also some leftover from the single-turn mindset. Early on, a lot of training data treated each response as a self-contained deliverable, almost like the final answer to an exam question. But in a real conversation, it's often better to give a short answer and let the person ask for more. That's a different style, and it requires the model to be comfortable leaving things out, trusting there'll be another turn.

And then there's caution. A lot of the extra length is disclaimers and caveats, which come from trying to avoid being wrong or causing harm. Some of that is valuable, but it accumulates and gets annoying.

None of these are fundamental. They're fixable with better data, better reward models, and more attention to what users actually want in context rather than in a side-by-side comparison. It's just that verbosity is an easy failure mode to slip into, and you have to push against it deliberately.

r001.rationale: The response says side-by-side raters often prefer longer, more thorough answers, which can lead training to favor verbosity.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention infrequent stop sequences during pretraining.

r003.rationale: It contrasts self-contained answers with short conversational replies, but does not explain that isolated-message evaluation makes the brief replies seem less complete.

r004.rationale: The response does not discuss instant text versus waiting for streamed text.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think there are a few things going on. The most obvious one is the training signal. When you do RLHF, you have humans comparing two responses, and there's a pretty consistent bias where the longer, more thorough-looking answer wins the comparison. Even if the rater would actually prefer a shorter answer in their day-to-day usage, when you put two responses side by side, the one that covers more ground, adds caveats, has nice structure with bullet points—that one tends to look more impressive. So the model learns that length is rewarded, and you get this ratchet effect.

The second thing is that verbosity is kind of a hedge against being wrong. If the model gives a short, direct answer and it's wrong, that's very visible. If it gives a long answer that covers five possibilities, one of them is probably right, and the rater is more forgiving. So there's an asymmetry in how errors get punished. Short and wrong is bad; long and partially right feels okay. The model picks up on that.

Then there's the fact that preferences are really heterogeneous. Some people genuinely want the full explanation, especially if they're learning something or don't know the domain. Other people are experts who just want the one-line answer. When you train a single model on a mix of these preferences, you end up at some average that's too long for the experts and maybe fine for everyone else. And the people who complain loudly about verbosity tend to be the power users, who are a minority of the actual population. So in some sense the model is calibrated to the median user, and the median user isn't the one posting on Twitter about it.

I'd also say we're just not that good yet at having the model infer what the user wants from context. Ideally the model would notice, "this person asked a very terse question, they probably want a terse answer," or "this person has been asking expert-level questions for ten turns, I can skip the background." That kind of adaptation is possible, and models do some of it, but it's not reliable. And you can always tell the model to be brief, and it will be for a turn or two, and then it drifts back. That drift is itself a training artifact—the prior toward length is strong enough that it reasserts itself.

The last thing I'd mention is that it's actually hard to measure. Verbosity doesn't show up well in benchmarks. If you're optimizing for accuracy on some eval, extra words are free or even helpful. So unless you deliberately build in a penalty for length, or you're measuring something like user satisfaction over many sessions, it doesn't get fixed. I think it is getting better—people are aware of it and are explicitly targeting it now—but it's one of those things where the default pressures all push in one direction, and you have to actively push back.

r001.rationale: It says human raters comparing responses tend to favor longer, more thorough-looking answers, rewarding length.

r002.rationale: It does not mention stop sequences or pretraining.

r003.rationale: It describes comparison bias toward longer answers, but does not explain how isolated-message evaluation disadvantages brief answers that depend on further interaction.

astra-6.text:
I think part of it is that verbosity is easier to reward than concision. If you’re comparing two answers, the longer one might include an extra caveat or an example that seems useful. So you pick it, even though, as a user, you might have preferred something you could read in five seconds.

There’s also an asymmetry: leaving out something important is a fairly obvious mistake. Adding another paragraph that’s sort of relevant doesn’t look as clearly wrong. So training can push the model toward covering all its bases.

The harder thing is figuring out what this particular user needs right now. Sometimes a one-sentence answer is exactly right, and sometimes it’s unhelpful. You want the model to make that distinction, rather than just learn a general preference for longer or shorter answers.

r001.rationale: It says that when comparing answers, people may choose the longer one because it includes useful-seeming caveats or examples, pushing training toward verbosity.

r002.rationale: It does not mention infrequent stop sequences during pretraining.

r003.rationale: It describes omissions as more visibly wrong than extra relevant material, but does not explain how isolated-message evaluation favors exhaustive answers over brief answers that depend on further interaction.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss users tolerating verbosity because text appears instantly rather than streaming.

sol-6.1.text:
I think part of it is that verbosity is easier to reward than conciseness. If you’re comparing two answers, the longer one might contain some extra detail that seems useful, and it’s easy to give it credit for that. It’s harder to account for the cost of making someone read all of it. So you can end up with a training signal that favors longer answers, even when users would prefer something shorter.

There’s also uncertainty about what the user wants. If you don’t know their background or exactly why they’re asking, covering more possibilities can seem like the safer choice. Ideally, the model would give a short answer and let the user ask for more. But getting that judgment right—what to leave out, when to stop—is a real part of being helpful.
